sections.html:
• Name: Panda crab
  • Other names: Sarawak land crab
  • Scientific name: Lepidothelphusa padawan
  • Minimum tank size: ~20 litres
  • Type: Semi-terrestrial
  • Breeding: Medium
  • Carapace size: up to 1 – 1.5 cm
  • Leg span: 3 – 4 cm
  • KH: 0 – 10
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 3 years
  • Colour: white – dark purple to black pattern

Many sources list this crab as Lepidothelphusa cognettii, but this is incorrect. Panda crabs are Lepidothelphusa padawan, according to the scientific studies in which the species was described. L. padawan can be easily distinguished from L. cognettii and congeners by its distinctive white – dark purple to black body in life. L. cognettii is almost cream-white, with light yellow anterior regions and chelipeds, and light blue posterior regions.

The name Lepidothelphusa comes from the ancient Greek "lepidos" (scale), referring to the scales covering the carapace, and "Thelphusa", the name of a genus of freshwater crabs. The species is named after Padawan, the area where it was collected.
This crab has only been described from one location: Kampung Sentah in the Padawan District of Sarawak, Malaysia.
These crabs inhabit damp rocks and leaf litter in partially shaded forest springs. The mudstone substrate in this area lies at an elevation of 100 to 300 metres above sea level.

Panda crabs need less space than most other crabs. For example, a tank of about 20 litres with lots of hiding places can house 3 adult crabs (1 male and 2 females). Unless the tank is larger, males should not be kept together because of potential territorial fights.

Larger tanks make it easier to build a paludarium with diverse areas for them to live in. It is all about hiding places. Panda crabs are great escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Land vs water: these are semi-terrestrial crabs, not fully aquatic. Ideally, land should take up at least 50 – 70% of the space in the tank, as in nature they mostly live on moist banks.

Water bowl

Panda crabs do not need a lot of water. They are fine with a suitably sized bowl of freshwater available 24/7.

  • The water only needs to be a few centimetres deep (about 5 – 8 cm), but deep enough to completely submerge the crab.
  • The bowl should be big enough for at least half of the crabs to fit in at the same time.
  • It should also have some hiding places.
  • Provide a variety of surfaces for them to get out of the water. Rocks or driftwood in the water can create small islands the crabs can climb onto.

Important: panda crabs cannot stay in the water all the time. They will drown. They need freshwater only. If you use tap water, add Seachem Prime to remove chlorine and chloramine; it also binds heavy metals and any ammonia, nitrite or nitrate for up to 48 hours.

Pros of water bowls: water changes are very easy and simple, and no filter is needed to keep the water clean and non-toxic. Cons: bowls usually do not look great in the setup unless you know how to decorate and hide them, and the water must be replaced every 2 – 3 days.

Classic paludarium setup

If you do not want to use a water bowl and prefer a classic paludarium setup, keep in mind their preferences (see water conditions). If the pH is too low, the crabs may become lethargic.

Humidity

Humidity is very important. Panda crabs need moist, humid air to breathe. In their natural environment, average humidity is around 75 – 85% throughout the year, higher in the rainy season. An ideal range is 70 – 90%. Humidity is adjusted by changing moisture and ventilation. This is normally a trial-and-error process, so expect some adjusting to get it right.

Rules for care and handling

  • Panda crabs are not pets to play with. Do not take them out just because you want to.
  • Never lift them by their legs or claws.
  • Do not leave uneaten food for too long, as it causes smell and bacteria. These crabs like to store uneaten food in their burrows.
  • Provide as many hiding places as you can.
  • Keep the temperature warm and humidity high.
  • Keep the lid tightly closed so they cannot escape.

Moulting

Periodic moulting is vital for the growth of all crustaceans: the old mineralised exoskeleton is completely replaced with a new one. The process has 4 phases: pre-molt, molt, post-molt and inter-molt.

  • Never disturb crabs while they are moulting.
  • Do not panic if you do not see them for several days; the cycle may last days. This is the most stressful moment in their life.
  • Keep putting and replacing food in the tank.
  • Keep giving calcium-rich food.
  • Do not remove the old exoskeleton from the tank. It consists of calcified chitin, protein and many minerals, and the crab will eat it later.

• pH: 7.0 – 8.0
  • Temperature: 24 – 28°C. In their natural habitat the average temperature ranges from about 22°C to 32°C.
  • Hardness: KH 0 – 10, GH 4 – 16
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm

Crabs are cold-blooded, so their body temperature depends entirely on the environment. When body temperature drops, metabolism slows, and temperature shock may occur if it drops too quickly or too far.

• Substrate: to replicate their natural environment, use coconut fibre, soil or peat; smooth gravel and sand can be used for the aquatic section. A very deep substrate is not needed; 5 – 7 cm is usually enough.
  • Heating: a heat mat placed under the tank can maintain the temperature and help prevent temperature shock.
  • Lighting: no special requirements, as the crabs are nocturnal. If you have plants, adapt the lighting to their needs; otherwise it may not be needed at all.
  • Decorations and hiding spots: panda crabs need a great many hiding places, including in the water. The more hiding places there are, the more active they become, because crabs that feel insecure hide more. Use live plants, PVC pipes, bark, driftwood, stones, nets, porous bricks and other decorations. Moss is a particularly favoured hiding spot.

Panda crabs are opportunistic omnivores that eat animal and plant material, dead or alive. They will eat just about any food they find on the bottom of the tank. For best growth, food should contain about 30 – 40% protein.

In captivity they eat a wide variety of foods:

  • Vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Detritus, leaf litter, seeds
  • Detritus worms, tubifex worms, blackworms, bloodworms, earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp, etc.

Foods they particularly enjoy: shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, shrimp food (such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine) and frozen bloodworms.

Although they are not picky, do not feed the same thing every day, as it can make them sick and shorten their lifespan. They need a balanced diet of protein (the main part), vegetables and fruits, and calcium.

Calcium is a crucial component of the shell, cellular function and overall health. A deficiency can cause weakness and cracks in the shell, making the crab susceptible to disease, heat and dehydration. Sources of calcium: kale, broccoli, spinach, cuttlebones, eggshells, figs, nuts, wonder shells, oyster shells, seaweed, seeds, insects, etc. A few small pieces of cuttlefish bone should be in the tank all the time.

Do not let them starve; otherwise, despite their peaceful temper and small size, they can even become cannibals.

  • Diet type: Omnivore
  • Feeding frequency: 3 – 4 times a week

Food can be left for 24 hours before it is removed, to prevent mould. It is best to feed in the evening or at night, since they are nocturnal and naturally eat while others sleep.

The behaviour of this crab has not been extensively studied, but the available information suggests that panda crabs have complex social relationships. They can be found in groups, although males may occasionally act aggressively toward one another.

They are primarily active at night, but they are not very shy, especially in large groups, and can even come out during the day. Nocturnal behaviour is common among small invertebrates and is mainly associated with avoiding visual predators while feeding; they are simply less active during the day.

Panda crabs are not diggers in the true sense, but they can push out some soil to make their own dens, which in nature they usually do at the edge of water bodies. Overall they are generally not burrowers.

  • Social: yes
  • Active: yes
  • Peaceful: yes (generally)
  • Burrowers: no (generally)

• Size: males are generally larger than females, but because of their small size the difference can be hard to notice.
  • Abdomen: males have a narrow, slim (triangular) plate, while females have a broad plate on the belly.
  • Colour: males have an almost or entirely white carapace, dark purple (almost black) walking legs, white chelipeds and at least three distinctive white – dark purple/black patterns on the carapace. Females are usually uniformly dark brown to purplish-brown to black, with cream-white chelipeds.
  • Claws: the fingers of the adult major male chela have the widest gape compared to other species in the genus Lepidothelphusa.

When a female is ready to mate, she signals receptiveness by allowing a male to approach. During mating the male takes a dominant position, flipping the female upside down and wrapping his body around her to fertilise. The process typically lasts several minutes.

Lepidothelphusa is a true freshwater crab genus. They do not need to return to the sea to release eggs and larvae, and this species has direct development. Females can carry about 20 – 40 eggs. The eggs hatch into miniature versions of the adult, and the females brood the juveniles for short periods before releasing them.

Tank mates

The ideal situation for panda crabs is a species tank. They can be kept in a group relatively safely, but only under certain conditions:

  • A ratio of 1 male to 3 females. In small enclosures, males in particular are extremely likely to fight.
  • The tank should have lots and lots of hiding places.

In a large paludarium it is possible to keep dwarf shrimp and small fish with them, as these crabs do not spend much time in the water.

Bad tank mates

  • Any crayfish species
  • Other crab species
  • Frogs

Plant safety

Yes, these crabs are safe to keep in planted paludariums. They usually do not uproot or cut plants.

Lifespan

There is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. In captivity they can live up to 2 – 3 years if appropriately cared for.

Sexual maturity and conclusion

Panda crabs are tiny, semi-terrestrial crabs well suited to small paludariums. They are excellent scavengers and require minimal care.
